title: Nonlocal fractional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang dynamics of grain boundaries
abstract: The kinetic roughening of driven grain boundaries (GBs) is fundamentally mediated by the collective behavior of disconnections, whose long-range $1/r$ elastic interactions distinguish them from conventional growing surfaces. Through large-scale molecular dynamics simulations and a nonlocal fractional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (fKPZ) theory, we demonstrate that driven GBs undergo a sharp transition of morphology at the yield point, from the quenched Edwards-Wilkinson universality class ($H \approx 0.33$) to an anomalous fKPZ regime ($H \approx 0.8$), while the 1/r nonlocal elasticity manifests as the fractional relaxation of GB morphology. The results show that the avalanche noise arrests the gradient catastrophe induced by the KPZ nonlinearity. Governed by the nonlocal elastic kernels, the resulting morphology breaks the Gaussian self-affinity and parallels the universality class of dynamic fracture.
summary: This work models the kinetic roughening of grain boundaries under strain, showing that long-range elastic interactions fundamentally alter surface growth universality. The system transitions sharply from an Edwards-Wilkinson state to a super-rough fKPZ regime ($H \approx 0.8$) upon yielding. This anomalous scaling links GB dynamics directly to the physics observed in dynamic fracture fronts.
main_problem: The study investigates the kinetic roughening of driven grain boundaries (GBs), which are governed by long-range $1/r$ elastic interactions from disconnections, distinguishing it from conventional surface growth models.
main_result: The system exhibits a sharp transition in morphology upon yielding, moving from a sub-diffusive Edwards-Wilkinson class ($H \approx 0.33$) to an anomalous fractional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (fKPZ) regime ($H \approx 0.8$).
method: The research combines large-scale Molecular Dynamics simulations with theoretical derivation of the governing Stochastic Partial Differential Equation (SPDE), mapping $1/r$ elasticity onto a fractional Laplacian.
model_or_system: The physical system is grain boundaries in polycrystalline materials subjected to constant strain-rate shear loading. The dynamics are modeled by an overdamped Langevin equation for discrete disconnections, which is coarse-grained into the fKPZ equation.
key_observables: Hurst exponent ($H$), universality classes (EW, KPZ), and the evolution of roughness with applied strain/time.
important_parameters: Strain rate ($\dot{\gamma}$), Temperature ($T$), Nonlocal elastic interaction strength ($1/r$ kernel).
main_assumptions: The theory assumes that $1/r$ elasticity can be mapped onto a fractional Laplacian operator, and the analysis relies on mapping GB dynamics to known universality classes like dynamic fracture.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the evolution of the Hurst exponent ($H$) across pre-yield ($H \approx 0.33$) and post-yield ($H \approx 0.8$) regimes. Figure 3 shows temperature-dependent stress-strain responses, confirming non-Arrhenius behavior.
paper_structure: The paper develops by first establishing the physical model (MD simulations of GBs), deriving the continuum equation (fKPZ) from discrete dynamics, analyzing the pre-yield and post-yield regimes separately using spectral analysis, and finally comparing the resulting anomalous scaling to dynamic fracture universality classes.
why_interesting: The connection between non-local elastic interactions in solid mechanics (GB motion/fracture) and universal growth equations like KPZ provides a rich platform for studying non-equilibrium dynamics far from equilibrium, relevant to understanding complex interfaces in condensed matter.
